core: Africa beyond ancient Egypt had many sophisticated, literate and organized states; the claim that Africa 'had no history' is false and is refuted by archaeology, Arabic-language written accounts, oral tradition (griots/jeliw), and manuscript libraries

The Sahel and the trans-Saharan gold-salt trade: camel caravans (regular long-distance trade from the 8th century CE) linked West African goldfields to North Africa, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East, exchanging West African gold for Saharan salt and spreading Islam along the routes
Ghana (Wagadu), flourishing c. 6th-13th centuries CE, grew rich taxing the gold-salt trade and declined by the end of the 12th century
Mali Empire (c. 1235-1600): founded when Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso kingdom in 1235; capital Niani; controlled the Sahelian trade cities Timbuktu, Djenne, and Gao
Mansa Musa (r. 1312-1337) made his famous hajj to Mecca in 1324, distributing so much gold that its value in Cairo fell for about twelve years, and he built mosques and schools at Timbuktu
Timbuktu became a celebrated center of Islamic learning (Sankore mosque and schools, manuscript libraries), thriving under Mali and Songhai into the 16th-17th centuries

Songhai Empire (c. 1460-1591), capital Gao: Sunni Ali (r. 1464-1492) built it by conquest; Askia Muhammad/Askia the Great (r. 1494-1528) organized its administration and Islamic law; it fell to a Moroccan invasion armed with muskets in 1590-1591

Kingdom of Aksum (in modern Ethiopia/Eritrea), c. 1st century CE to c. 7th-8th century CE, peak 3rd-6th centuries: Red Sea trading power through the port of Adulis, minted its own coins, and under King Ezana adopted Christianity in the mid-4th century (c. 350 CE); its Christian tradition continued in the Ethiopian highlands

The Swahili coast: Muslim traders from Arabia and Egypt began settling from the 8th century; monsoon-driven Indian Ocean trade produced, by the 1200s, a distinct Swahili civilization of independent, Islamic, commercially oriented city-states (e.g. Kilwa) speaking a Bantu language with heavy Arabic borrowing

Great Zimbabwe: a stone-built city of the Shona (Bantu-speaking) people, inhabited c. 1100-c. 1450 (occupation extending to c. 1550), peak c. 1300-1450, famous for massive mortarless dry-stone granite walls (the Great Enclosure); it grew wealthy on gold and cattle and traded through the Swahili port of Kilwa/Sofala into the Indian Ocean network
Islam and long-distance trade were unifying threads across many of these states, but Africa was internally diverse in language, religion, and political form
supporting: Bantu-speaking peoples spread agriculture and ironworking across much of sub-Saharan Africa (dispersal especially c. 500-1000 CE), underlying later states
Aksum was the first sub-Saharan kingdom to mint its own coinage (gold, silver, bronze from the 3rd century CE) and among the earliest to adopt Christianity
Distinguishing established dates/sequence (fact) from interpretation of meaning; ancient/medieval dates given with 'c.' because scholarship gives ranges

Eyewitness written records exist, e.g. the Arab geographer al-Masudi (writing in 915) on the East African coast and the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta, who visited both the Swahili coast and Mali in the 14th century

claims.claim: The trans-Saharan trade that enriched West African states centered on exchanging West African gold for Saharan salt, carried by camel caravans that made regular long-distance trade possible from about the 8th century CE.
The Mali Empire was founded when Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso kingdom in 1235; its rulers controlled the trade cities of Timbuktu, Djenne, and Gao.
Mansa Musa ruled Mali from 1312 to 1337 and made a celebrated pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca in 1324-1325, distributing so much gold that its value in Cairo fell for about twelve years.
The Songhai Empire (c. 1460-1591), centered on Gao, was built by Sunni Ali (r. 1464-1492) and organized by Askia Muhammad (r. 1494-1528); it fell to a Moroccan invasion using firearms in 1590-1591.
Under Mali and Songhai, Timbuktu became a major center of Islamic learning, with the Sankore mosque, many Qur'anic schools, and manuscript libraries, thriving into the 16th-17th centuries.

The Kingdom of Aksum, in modern Ethiopia and Eritrea, flourished from about the 1st to the 6th-7th centuries CE, traded through the Red Sea port of Adulis, minted its own coins, and adopted Christianity in the mid-4th century (c. 350 CE) under King Ezana.

By the 1200s a distinct Swahili civilization of independent, Islamic, trade-oriented city-states (such as Kilwa) had emerged along the East African coast, speaking a Bantu language with heavy Arabic borrowing and participating in monsoon-driven Indian Ocean trade documented as early as al-Masudi in 915.

Great Zimbabwe was a Shona (Bantu-speaking) stone-built city inhabited c. 1100-c. 1450 (peak c. 1300-1450), famous for massive mortarless dry-stone granite walls, that grew wealthy on gold and cattle and traded through the Swahili port of Kilwa into the Indian Ocean network.

The idea that sub-Saharan Africa 'had no history' is false: these states left written records (Arabic accounts, the Timbuktu manuscripts), oral traditions preserved by griots, and monumental archaeology such as Great Zimbabwe and the Aksum stelae.
Islam and long-distance trade were common threads across many of these states, yet Africa remained internally diverse in language, religion, and political organization.

positions: World History Encyclopedia: the old Aksum empire had ceased to exist by the late 8th century CE
OpenStax repeats a tradition that the Christian kingdom fell to the Zagwe queen Gudit in the 10th century
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a decline over the 7th-8th centuries with the Christian tradition continuing in the Ethiopian highlands; the 10th-century 'Gudit' story is flagged as tradition rather than a firm date, so the lesson gives Aksum's floruit as c. 1st-7th/8th centuries CE.
